game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
The expected sum of three fair dice is 10.5, so I centre the quote there. Informed traders only buy when the sum is high and only sell when it is low, so I widen the spread to cover that adverse selection.

I estimated expected profit per side by comparing noise-trader gains with informed-trader losses. For the ask:

| Ask | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 12.0 | about 0.15 |
| 13.0 | about 0.35 |
| 13.5 | about 0.40 |
| 14.0 | about 0.43 |
| 14.5 | about 0.43 |

Profit is nearly flat beyond 13.5. I choose 13.5 for the ask so I still get fills, and mirror it on the bid at 7.5.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

My fair value estimate is about 9.3, below the prior of 10.5. The prior is the three-dice mean, 10.5. The counterparty sold to me at 7.5, which is more likely if the true sum is low.

- **Informed seller:** the informed share of that sale is about 26%, and an informed seller's sum is below 7.5, averaging about 6.0.
- **Noise seller:** a noise seller carries no information about the dice, so the expected sum stays at 10.5.
- **Blend:** 0.26 × 6.0 + 0.74 × 10.5 ≈ 9.3.

I'm long 1, so I skew the quotes slightly toward selling. The ask sits a little above fair value and the bid a bit further below it, to cover adverse selection from informed traders.

{"bid": 7.9, "ask": 11.0}

Fair value is 12: die 1 is 5, and the other two dice add an expected 7. I'm at position 0, so no inventory skew is needed.

The informed trader (35%) knows the sum, which ranges from 7 to 17. A tight spread loses a lot to them. A wide spread gives up some noise-trader volume (noise std 4.4) but avoids most of that loss. My rough per-side expected profit at different half-spreads around 12:

| Half-spread | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | about 0.08 |
| 2.0 | about 0.32 |
| 3.0 | about 0.45 |
| 4.0 | about 0.46 |

The gain flattens out around a half-spread of 3, so I'll quote there.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 15.0}

Fair value is 5 + 3.5 + 3.5 = 12, since die 1 is 5 and the other two dice average 3.5 each.

An informed trader knows die 2 + die 3, so the settlement value lies between 7 and 17. I estimated my expected profit per quote at several ask prices, with the bid symmetric around 12:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 13 | about +0.08 |
| 14 | about +0.38 |
| 14.5 | about +0.45 |
| 15 | about +0.48 |
| 16 | about +0.47 |

The profit per quote is flat from roughly 14.5 to 16. I'm long +1, so I want to lean toward selling and keep room to buy later. I'm quoting a slightly tighter ask than a symmetric spread would give, and a bid slightly closer to 12 than the 9.0 optimum.

{"bid": 9.4, "ask": 14.2}

Die 1 = 5 and die 2 = 4 are known, so the settlement value is 9 plus die 3. That puts the public fair value at 9 + 3.5 = 12.5. An informed trader knows the final value is one of 10 to 15, each equally likely.

I compared expected profit per quote against 12.5 for a range of asks. The bid side mirrors this around 12.5.

| Ask | Approx. expected profit vs. 12.5 |
|---|---|
| 13.0 | −0.03 |
| 13.5 | +0.15 |
| 14.0 | +0.30 |
| 14.5 | +0.39 |
| 15.0 | +0.46 |
| 15.5 | +0.48 |
| 16.0 | +0.49 |
| 16.5 | +0.47 |

Profit is flat from about 15 to 16, so the exact ask there matters little. The symmetric bid would sit near 9 to 9.5.

I am long 1, so I would like to sell a little more than I buy. I therefore set the ask slightly toward fair value at 15.0 and keep the bid at 9.5 rather than lowering it.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 15.0}

Fair value is 5 + 4 + 3.5 = 12.5, since only die 3 is unknown. An informed trader knows the settlement value is one of 10 to 15. A noise trader values the contract at 12.5 plus Normal(0, 4.4) noise.

This is the last quote, so I only need to maximise expected profit on this one trade and can ignore later effects. I compared candidate prices by the expected edge per quote, weighting informed trades (35%) and noise trades (65%).

- **Ask:** the expected edge keeps rising as I widen out to about 15.8–16, where it is roughly 0.48, and then falls. Below that, informed buyers take too much of the edge. Above it, noise trades become too rare.
- **Bid:** the setup is symmetric around 12.5, so the best bid is about 9.0–9.2.

I'll quote slightly inside those optima.

info.raw:
Before any dice are revealed, the fair value is 3 × 3.5 = 10.5. I picked the half-spread by comparing the expected profit per side at different widths. Each side earns from noise traders (35% informed, 65% noise, noise standard deviation 4.4) and loses to informed traders, who know the sum.

| Half-spread | Net expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | about 0 |
| 1.5 | about 0.15 |
| 2.5 | about 0.35 |
| 3.5 | about 0.43 |
| 4.0 | about 0.43 |
| 4.5 | about 0.42 |

The profit is flat between 3.5 and 4.0, so I take 3.5. That gives a bid of 7.0 and an ask of 14.0.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 14.0}

Fair value is 10.5, the expected sum of three dice. Informed traders know the exact sum, so I need a spread wide enough to cover adverse selection.

I estimated the expected profit per side at a half-spread d around 10.5, combining the noise-trader fill probability (sd 4.4) with the informed-trader loss:

| d | Net expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 1 | about 0 |
| 2 | about 0.26 |
| 3 | about 0.40 |
| 4 | about 0.43 |

The edge is nearly flat between d=3 and d=4. The previous quote (7 / 14) got no fill, so I'll tighten slightly to d=3 and improve the chance of a trade.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

Die 1 is 4, so the public fair value is 4 + 3.5 + 3.5 = 11.

An informed trader knows dice 2 and 3 exactly, so its value is 4 + (die 2 + die 3), which ranges from 6 to 16. A noise trader values the contract at 11 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 4.4.

I compared ask levels by expected profit per quote. The gain from noise traders buying above fair value outweighs the loss to informed traders, and the net profit peaks around an ask of 14 to 14.5:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 12 | about +0.07 |
| 13 | about +0.32 |
| 14 | about +0.45 |
| 14.5 | about +0.49 |
| 15 | about +0.47 |

The bid side mirrors this around 11, so I'm quoting 8 and 14. That is a wide spread, symmetric about fair value, which protects against informed traders while still catching noise flow.

{"bid": 8, "ask": 14}

Die 1 is 4, so the fair value is 4 + 3.5 + 3.5 = 11. No trades so far, so there is no extra information from the history.

Widening the quote helps against the informed trader (probability 0.35), who knows the exact sum. For asks, I computed my expected profit per quote at several levels from 12 to 15:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 12 | about 0.07 |
| 13 | about 0.32 |
| 14 | about 0.445 |
| 14.5 | about 0.485 |
| 15 | about 0.47 |

This is flat between 13.5 and 15, so I'm quoting somewhat inside the myopic optimum to improve the chance of a trade. The bid mirrors the ask around 11.

{"bid": 8.3, "ask": 13.7}

Dice 1 and 2 sum to 10, so the settlement value is 10 plus die 3. Die 3 averages 3.5, so the public fair value is 13.5, and the settlement range is 11 to 16.

An informed trader only buys from me if the value is above my ask, and only sells to me if it is below my bid. Setting the ask at 16.5 or higher and the bid at 10.5 or lower means informed traders can never trade profitably against me, since the value never goes above 16 or below 11. I then earn only from noise traders, whose valuation is 13.5 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 4.4.

Checking half-spreads around 13.5, the expected profit per side is roughly:

| Half-spread | Ask / bid | Profit per side |
|---|---|---|
| 2.0 | 15.5 / 11.5 | 0.39 |
| 2.5 | 16 / 11 | 0.46 |
| 3.0 | 16.5 / 10.5 | 0.48 |
| 3.5 | 17 / 10 | 0.485 |
| 4.0 | 17.5 / 9.5 | 0.47 |

Profit is flat around a half-spread of 3 to 3.5. I'll quote 3.2 either side of 13.5, which gives an ask of 16.7 and a bid of 10.3.

{"bid": 10.3, "ask": 16.7}

Die 1 and die 2 total 10, so the settlement value is 10 + die 3, which is 11 to 16 with a mean of 13.5. This is the last quote, so there is no inventory risk beyond this trade.

At an ask of 16 or higher, an informed buyer never trades profitably, because the highest possible value is 16. The only fills are noise traders, who buy when 13.5 + noise exceeds my ask. Expected profit on the ask is about 0.65 × P(noise above ask) × (ask − 13.5).

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 16 | ≈ 0.46 |
| 16.8 | ≈ 0.49 |
| 17.5 | ≈ 0.47 |

The curve peaks near 16.8. The bid side is symmetric around 13.5, so the best bid is about 10.2.

{"bid": 10.2, "ask": 16.8}

I set a symmetric quote around 8 with half-spread h and estimated the expected profit per side. A noise trader (valuation Normal(8, 3)) pays me h whenever it trades. An informed trader costs me the amount by which the settlement value passes my price. Die 2 + die 3 − 7 is triangular on −5..5, which gives the informed loss.

| h | Net expected profit per side |
|---|---|

| 2.0 | 0.23 |
| 2.5 | 0.26 |
| 3.0 | 0.27 |

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 11.0}

Die 1 and die 2 sum to 7, so the settlement value is 7 plus die 3, which is uniform on 8 to 13. The fair value is 10.5.

I compared symmetric quotes around 10.5 by expected profit per quote (informed buyers take the ask only when the settlement value is above it, and noise traders use 10.5 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 3):

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 13.0}

Die 1 and die 2 are revealed as 1 and 6, so the settlement value is 7 + die 3, which is between 8 and 13. The fair value is 10.5.

For each side I compared the expected loss to an informed trader (who knows the exact value) with the expected gain from a noise trader (valuation about 10.5 ± 3). The ask is the mirror image of the bid.

- At an ask of 13.0, an informed trader never buys, because the value cannot exceed 13. A noise trader buys with probability about 0.20 and pays 2.5 above fair value. That gives roughly +0.33 per quote.
- Lowering the ask to 12.5 gives roughly +0.30, and 12.0 gives roughly +0.24. Raising it to 13.5 gives roughly +0.31.
- By symmetry, a bid of 8.0 is best on the other side, also at roughly +0.33.

The best quote is therefore the edge of the possible range on each side: 8.0 and 13.0.

| d | Expected profit |

info.raw:
The contract settles at the maximum of three dice. I computed the distribution of that maximum from the product of the three dice's cumulative probabilities.

**Settlement distribution**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 4 | 0.075 |
| 6 | 0.100 |
| 7 | 0.0875 |
| 8 | 0.2625 |
| 9 | 0.075 |
| 12 | 0.400 |

The public fair value (the mean) is about 9.09.

**Ask.** The distribution is skewed: 40% of the time the value is 12. An informed buyer who knows the value is 12 costs me money at any ask below 12. I tested asks from 10 to 12 using the noise-trader fill chance (SD 2.6) and the informed loss, and expected profit per quote peaks near 11.8.

**Bid.** Informed sellers hit me when the value is 4, 6 or 7. Expected profit per quote is highest around a bid of 7. I shade slightly lower, to 6.9.

{"bid": 6.9, "ask": 11.8}

Fair value is about 9.09, the expected maximum of the three dice. The distribution of the maximum is:

| Max | 4 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.075 | 0.100 | 0.0875 | 0.2625 | 0.075 | 0.400 |

The distribution is skewed, with a 40% chance the maximum is 12. That makes the informed trader costly on the ask side. I compared expected profit across candidate prices, counting noise-trader flow and informed-trader losses:

- **Ask:** expected profit is flat at roughly 0.30 per quote between about 11.4 and 11.9. Lower asks lose more to informed buyers.
- **Bid:** expected profit is highest at about 7.0, roughly 0.29 per quote. Higher bids give up more to informed sellers.

I'm quoting 7.0 / 11.4.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.4}

Die 3 = 1, so the contract settles at max(die 1, die 2, 1). Die 1 is 2, 4, 8 or 8 and die 2 is 4, 6, 7 or 12, so die 3 can't set the maximum.

The settlement value then has these probabilities:

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 4 | 2/16 |
| 6 | 2/16 |
| 7 | 2/16 |
| 8 | 6/16 |
| 12 | 4/16 |

The public fair value is the mean, 8.125.

I compared expected profit per quote at several prices, counting noise traders (valuation 8.125 plus noise with standard deviation 2.6) and informed traders (20%) who know the exact value.

- **Ask:** informed buyers only hurt me when the value is 12. Expected profit is about 0.25 per quote at 10.0 to 11.0 and peaks near 10.5, so I'll quote 10.4.
- **Bid:** informed sellers only hurt me at the low values 4 and 6. Expected profit is about 0.30 per quote around 5.8 to 6.0, so I'll quote 6.0.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.4}

Die 3 came up 1, so the contract settles at max(die 1, die 2), since die 1's lowest face is 2.

The 16 equally likely (die 1, die 2) pairs give these settlement values:
- 4: 2/16
- 6: 2/16
- 7: 2/16
- 8: 6/16
- 12: 4/16

The mean is 130/16 = 8.125, which is the public fair value.

I quoted around that fair value, with a spread wide enough to cover the 20% chance of an informed trader:
- **Ask:** the expected edge peaks around 10.5. I shaded it slightly lower, to 10.2, because I'm short and don't want to add to that position.
- **Bid:** the edge peaks around 6 to 6.5. I raised it to 6.7 because buying would reduce my short position.

{"bid": 6.7, "ask": 10.2}

With die 3 = 1 and die 1 = 8, the settlement value is 8 unless die 2 shows 12. So it is 8 with probability 3/4 and 12 with probability 1/4, giving a fair value of 9.0.

- **Ask:** An informed buyer only buys when the value is 12. A noise trader's valuation is 9 plus noise with standard deviation 2.6. Expected profit is highest for asks around 11–11.5, so I'll quote 11.2.
- **Bid:** Below 8, an informed seller never hits me, because the value is at least 8. Noise sellers give the best expected profit for bids around 7–7.5, so I'll quote 7.3. Being short 2, I'm happy to buy back at that price.

{"bid": 7.3, "ask": 11.2}

Die 1 = 8 and die 3 = 1, so the contract settles at max(8, die 2). Die 2 is 12 with probability 1/4, and otherwise the settlement is 8. The expected settlement value, and so the public fair value, is 0.75×8 + 0.25×12 = 9.

This is the last quote, so I just maximise expected edge against that value of 9. A noise trader's valuation is 9 + N(0, 2.6). An informed trader knows the value is 8 or 12.

- **Ask:** The expected profit is about 0.31 at an ask of 11.4–11.5. It falls off on both sides of that range, since a lower ask is picked off by informed buyers when the value is 12. I pick 11.4.
- **Bid:** The expected profit is flat at about 0.35 for bids of 6.9–7.2, and it falls once the bid goes above 8, where informed sellers hit it when the value is 8. I pick 7.0.

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 12 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 1, 4 cards worth 3, 3 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Opening quote: a wide spread, with the bid near the lowest card value and the ask near the second-highest.

**Settlement distribution.** There are C(12,3) = 220 possible hands. The minimum card has these probabilities:
- Min = 1: 55/220 (25%)
- Min = 3: 130/220 (59%)
- Min = 9: 31/220 (14%)
- Min = 14: 4/220 (1.8%)

The expected settlement value, and so the public fair value, is 780/220 ≈ 3.55.

**Ask.** An informed buyer takes my ask whenever the true value is 9 or 14, and I lose money on each of those trades. A noise trader's valuation is the fair value plus noise with standard deviation 2.8, so noise buyers only pay up rarely at high prices. Working through the expected profit at several ask levels:
- At an ask of 4.5 to 7, the expected profit is negative.
- At an ask of about 8, the expected profit is roughly zero.
- At an ask of about 9, the expected profit is slightly positive.

I set the ask at 9.0.

**Bid.** An informed seller only hurts me when the true value is 1. A bid around 1.0 to 1.2 gives up almost nothing to informed sellers. It still captures noise sellers, who sell below the fair value of 3.55. The expected profit per quote peaks near a bid of 1.0 to 1.2, at roughly +0.22. Raising the bid much further adds adverse selection faster than it adds noise fills.

I set the bid at 1.2.

{"bid": 1.2, "ask": 9.0}

Before any cards are revealed, I price off the distribution of the minimum of 3 cards drawn from the 12.

- Out of 220 possible hands, the minimum is 1 in 55, 3 in 130, 9 in 31 and 14 in 4.
- That gives a prior expected value of about 3.55.
- My quote 1 (bid 1.2, ask 9) drew no trade. That mildly favours higher values, so my working estimate rises to about 3.8.

**Ask:** An informed buyer who knows the value is 9 or 14 costs me money at any ask below those values. Noise traders rarely pay much above 8. The expected edge is best near 9, so I keep the ask at 9.

**Bid:** Informed sellers know when the value is 1, so a higher bid costs me more there. Noise sellers fill only occasionally at low prices. A bid of about 1.5 balances the two.

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 9}

My fair value estimate is about 3.6. Here is how I got it.

- **Remaining deck:** With card 1 = 9, the other two cards come from 11 cards: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s.
- **Update from the trade history:** Someone sold at 1.5 after not selling at 1.2. That favours a hidden 1 somewhat. Posterior probabilities for the settlement value are roughly 35% for 1, 44% for 3 and 22% for 9, giving a mean of about 3.6.
- **Ask:** An informed buyer picks me off whenever the value is 9, so a low ask loses money. At 9.0 an informed buyer with value 9 does not trade. The only buyers are noise traders paying well above fair value.
- **Bid:** An informed seller with value 1 loses me money on anything above 1.0. At 1.0 an informed seller with value 1 does not trade, since its valuation is not strictly below my bid. Noise traders still sell at a discount to fair value.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

I quote a bid of 1.0 and an ask of 9. These come from the posterior on the settlement value.

**Remaining cards.** Card 1 is 9, so the other two cards come from the 11 left: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s. That gives 55 equally likely pairs.
- Value 1 if the pair contains the 1: 10 pairs.
- Value 3 if there is no 1 but at least one 3: 30 pairs.
- Value 9 otherwise: 15 pairs.

**Prior fair value.** (10×1 + 30×3 + 15×9) / 55 ≈ 4.27.

**Trade history.** The quote 2 sale at 1.5 points toward a low value. An informed seller only sells at 1.5 if the value is 1, while a noise trader needs a low valuation. I estimate this as roughly an 8:1 likelihood ratio in favour of value 1. The posterior is about 64% on value 1, 24% on value 3 and 12% on value 9. That gives a fair value of about 2.4.

**Bid.** At a bid of 1.0, an informed seller with value 1 gains nothing by selling, since the value is not below the bid. Noise sellers still hit it about 15% of the time, and I buy about 1.4 below fair. That gives an expected gain of roughly 0.22 per quote. A bid of 1.5 lets informed value-1 sellers hit me at a loss and has roughly zero expected value.

**Ask.** Any ask below 9 lets an informed buyer with value 9 take it at a large loss. At 9 informed traders cannot profit, and noise traders almost never reach it.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9}

Card 2 is the only 1 in the deck, so the smallest dealt card is certainly 1 and the contract settles at exactly 1.

- **Informed counterparty:** it values the contract at 1. It would only buy from me at an ask below 1 and only sell to me at a bid above 1. Quoting an ask above 1 and a bid below 1 means I never trade with an informed counterparty at a loss.
- **Noise trader:** its valuation is 1 + N(0, 2.8). If I quote x away from 1, the expected profit is about 0.5 · x · P(noise beyond x). This peaks at x ≈ 2.1, where the tail probability is about 0.23.
- **Ask:** 1 + 2.1 = 3.1.
- **Bid:** 1 − 2.1 = −1.1. I buy at that price only from noise sellers, which is still profitable because the contract settles at 1.

My position of +1 leaves room on both sides.

{"bid": -1.1, "ask": 3.1}

The settlement value is already known. Card 2 is the only 1 in the deck, so the minimum of the three cards is 1 whatever card 3 turns out to be. Quote 6 is the last quote, so I only need to maximise expected profit on this one trade.

- **Informed counterparty:** it values the contract at 1, so it will not buy above 1 or sell below 1.
- **Noise trader:** its valuation is 1 + N(0, 2.8), so it trades only when the price is far enough from 1.
- **Ask:** my edge at ask 1 + x is x · P(noise > x). This peaks at z = x/2.8 ≈ 0.75, so x ≈ 2.1 and the ask is about 3.1.
- **Bid:** the same logic applies below 1, giving a bid of about 1 − 2.1 = −1.1. A bid at or below 1 means the informed trader cannot profit from selling to me.
- **Position:** I am at +2, so one more buy takes me to +3, which is within the limit.

{"bid": -1.1, "ask": 3.1}

info.raw:
I priced off the expected settlement value and adjusted for the 20% informed traders.

**Fair value.** There are 28 possible pairs from the 8 cards.
- The minimum is 2 in 7 pairs, 9 in 11 pairs and 13 in 10 pairs.
- The expected minimum is (7·2 + 11·9 + 10·13) / 28 = 243/28 ≈ 8.68.

**Informed traders.** They know the value, which is 2 with probability 25%, 9 with 39% and 13 with 36%. They sell to a bid that is too high and buy from an ask that is too low.

**Choosing the spread.** I compared expected profit at different quotes, using noise traders with valuation around 8.68 and standard deviation 6.3.
- Ask: expected profit rises as the ask moves out, from about 0.38 at 10.5 to about 0.72 at 12 and about 0.85 at 13.
- Bid: expected profit is about 0.28 at 7, about 0.75 at 4 and about 0.79 at 3.

The profit-maximising quotes are therefore wide, roughly 3–4 on the bid and 13 on the ask. I pulled them in slightly to 4.5 and 12.5 to keep some flow.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 12.5}

My estimate of fair value is about 7.4.

- **Prior:** of the 28 equally likely card pairs, the minimum is 2 in 7, 9 in 11, and 13 in 10. That gives an expected settlement of 243/28 ≈ 8.68.
- **Update:** a counterparty sold to me at 4.5, which is more likely if the value is 2 (an informed seller) than otherwise. The posterior is roughly 40% on 2, 32% on 9 and 29% on 13, so fair value is about 7.4.
- **Ask:** I estimated expected profit per quote against noise traders and informed traders at several prices. It peaks around 12 to 13, because that is where noise-trader edge is large and informed traders rarely buy. Being long, I also prefer selling, so I post 12.0.
- **Bid:** the same calculation favours a low bid, since an informed seller only hits it when the value is 2. I post 4.0, slightly below my last fill, to limit adding to the long position.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 12.0}

The settlement value is already known. Card 1 is 2, and every remaining card is 9 or higher, so the minimum of the two cards is 2 for certain.

- **Informed counterparty:** it values the contract at 2, so I never want to sell to it below 2 or buy from it above 2.
- **Noise trader:** its valuation is Normal(2, 6.3), so I can take edge from it on both sides.
- **Best edge:** the edge x that maximises x·P(noise > x) is about 0.75 standard deviations, so x ≈ 4.7.
- **Prices:** that gives an ask of about 2 + 4.7 = 6.7 and a bid of about 2 − 4.7 = −2.7.

My position (+1) doesn't matter for risk, since the settlement value is certain, and I'm far from the ±5 limits.

{"bid": -2.7, "ask": 6.7}

The settlement value is already known. Card 1 is 2 and every other card is worth at least 9, so the smallest dealt card is 2 for certain.

- **Informed counterparty:** values the contract at exactly 2, so it never trades at a bid below 2 or an ask above 2.
- **Noise trader:** values it at 2 plus Normal(0, 6.3) noise, so it trades only when its noise carries it past my price.
- **Edge per trade:** a sale at ask a earns a − 2, and a purchase at bid b earns 2 − b.

With d the distance from 2, each side's expected profit is proportional to d × P(noise beyond d). This is maximised where 1 − Φ(x) = xφ(x), with x = d/6.3. That gives x ≈ 0.75, so d ≈ 4.7.

This is the last quote, so there is no future inventory to manage. The optimal prices are ask ≈ 6.7 and bid ≈ −2.7, the same as my previous quote.

The distribution is skewed: the settlement value is 15 about 40% of the time. An informed buyer who knows it is 15 would take my ask, so I keep the ask a little above fair value. An informed seller would hit my bid whenever the maximum is 10 or lower, which happens about 32% of the time, so I keep the bid below fair value as well. I quote roughly symmetrically around 12 with about a one-point margin on each side, which still lets noise traders (standard deviation 2.7) trade with me often.

With d = 2.7x, the expected profit is proportional to x·Φ(−x). Setting the derivative to zero gives Φ(−x) = x·φ(x), which holds at x ≈ 0.75, so d ≈ 2.0.

- **Bid:** 15 − 2.0 = 13.0. A fill also covers part of my short position.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The public fair value is 4.5, from 0.5 × 3 + 0.5 × 6. Informed traders know the exact value, which is 6 if the coin is all heads and otherwise averages 3. That creates adverse selection on both sides.

I compared expected profit per quote at several prices, counting noise traders (valuation 4.5 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.6) and informed traders separately.

- **Ask:** Profit peaks around 6.4 to 6.5, at roughly 0.35 per quote. At 6 or above, an informed buyer can never profit, because the value cannot exceed 6.
- **Bid:** Profit peaks around 2.3 to 2.5, at roughly 0.32 to 0.35 per quote. Informed sellers cost little at that level, since a low value is unlikely.

I'm quoting roughly symmetrically around 4.5.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 6.5}

I quote 2.9 / 6.2, around a fair value of 4.5.

- **Fair value:** the expected number of heads is 6 × (0.5 × 0.5 + 0.5 × 1) = 4.5.
- **Informed risk on the ask:** about half the time the coin is the all-heads one, so the value is 6. Selling below 6 loses money to an informed buyer, so the ask sits at or just above 6.
- **Informed risk on the bid:** the fair coin gives a binomial value centred on 3, so an informed seller hits any bid above about 3 at a loss. I set the bid near 3, where the noise-trader gain outweighs that loss.
- **Expected profit per quote:** I estimated this at a few tenths of a point on each side (about 0.3 at a bid of 3.0, about 0.34 at an ask of 6.0).

{"bid": 2.9, "ask": 6.2}

My estimate of the settlement value is 5.6, so I'm quoting a wide spread around it.

- **Posterior on the coin:** After two heads, P(biased coin) = 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.5 × 0.25) = 0.8.
- **Expected settlement:** 2 + 0.8 × 4 + 0.2 × 2 = 5.6.
- **Informed trader's value:** It is 6 if the coin is biased. If the coin is fair, it is 2 + Binomial(4, 0.5), which has mean 4.
- **Ask:** An informed buyer never pays above 6, so an ask above 6 only trades with noise traders. A myopic optimum is near 7.5, and I shade it to 7.2.
- **Bid:** The informed seller only hurts me when the coin is fair, which is rare. A myopic optimum is near 3.5, and I use 3.8.

{"bid": 3.8, "ask": 7.2}

Flips 1 and 2 are both heads, so the posterior that the coin is the all-heads one is 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.125) = 0.8. Each of the 4 unrevealed flips then has an expected value of 0.8·1 + 0.2·0.5 = 0.9, so the fair value is 2 + 4·0.9 = 5.6.

The settlement value can never exceed 6, so an informed trader never buys above 6. The earlier buy at 7.2 therefore came from a noise trader and tells us nothing new.

- **Ask:** Above 6 there is no adverse selection, only noise buyers. Expected profit per quote peaks around 7.3 to 7.5, so I ask 7.3.
- **Bid:** The informed side only sells when the value is below the bid, which happens only if the coin is fair and the remaining flips go badly. Expected profit is highest around 3.5 to 4.0. A bid of 4.0 also helps reduce the short position, so I bid 4.0.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.3}

Fair value: four heads in four flips makes the biased coin much more likely. P(biased) = 1 / (1 + 1/16) = 16/17. The two unrevealed flips then average 2 heads if the coin is biased and 1 if it is fair, so the expected settlement is 4 + 2·(16/17) + 1·(1/17) ≈ 5.94.

This is the last quote, so I only need to maximise the expected profit of this one round of trading. Inventory risk matters only through settlement.

- **Informed traders:** they know the value is 6 with probability about 96%. An ask of 6 or more, or a bid of 6 or less, rarely loses to them.
- **Ask:** I scanned asks against noise-trader fill probability times margin over 5.94. The expected profit peaks around 8.0 (about 0.354).
- **Bid:** by the same scan the bid peaks near 4.0 (about 0.354). At 4.0 the informed traders almost never sell to me, because their value is 4 only about 1.5% of the time and they need a valuation strictly below my bid.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 8.0}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value is 6 × (0.5·0.5 + 0.5·1) = 4.5. I'm quoting wide because 20% of counterparties know the settlement value, and the value is either 6 (the all-heads coin) or about 3 (the fair coin).

- **Ask:** an informed buyer takes me when the value is 6, so asking below 6 loses money on those trades. Noise-trader demand falls as the ask rises, and my estimated expected profit per quote peaks around 6.3–6.5 (about 0.35). I'll ask 6.4.
- **Bid:** an informed seller hits me when the value is below my bid. Balancing that against noise-trader flow, expected profit is flat at roughly 0.32 for bids between 2 and 2.5. I'll bid 2.4.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 6.4}

I set fair value at 4.5, which is half the weight on a fair coin (mean 3) plus half on an all-heads coin (6 heads).

I checked expected profit per quote for different asks and bids. This accounts for noise traders with a valuation of 4.5 plus noise, and for informed traders who know the settlement value.

- **Ask:** expected profit is nearly flat between about 6.0 and 6.6, at roughly 0.35. Below 6, informed traders who know the value is 6 start to cost more.
- **Bid:** expected profit peaks around 2.4, at roughly 0.33. Raising the bid toward 3 costs more to informed sellers.

I'll quote slightly tighter than the last quote, since the profit curve is flat there.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 6.3}

My estimate of the settlement value is 5.6, and I'm quoting wide because informed traders are a risk on the bid side.

- **Posterior on the coin:** Two heads in a row have likelihood 0.25 under the fair coin and 1 under the always-heads coin. That puts the always-heads coin at 1/(1+0.25) = 0.8.
- **Fair value:** The 2 revealed heads are certain. The remaining 4 flips average 0.8×4 + 0.2×2 = 3.6. Fair value is therefore 2 + 3.6 = 5.6.
- **Ask:** If the coin is always-heads, the contract settles at 6, so an informed buyer never pays more than 6. Pricing the ask at 6.3 means informed traders cannot profit from buying, and noise traders still buy at about 0.7 above fair value.
- **Bid:** If the coin is fair, the value could be as low as 2, so an informed seller could hit a bid near 5.6 for a large loss. I set the bid well below fair value at 4.2. That still earns a good margin from noise traders and limits the losses to informed sellers.

{"bid": 4.2, "ask": 6.3}

Four heads are revealed, so I update on which coin it is.

- The posterior probability of the fair coin is (1/32) / (1/32 + 1/2) = 1/17.
- The expected settlement value is 4 + 2 − 1/17 ≈ 5.94.
- The value is exactly 6 with probability about 0.956, and 4 or 5 otherwise.

**Ask:** An informed buyer can never profit above 6.0, because the value is at most 6. The ask is therefore only exposed to noise traders. Expected profit from noise traders, 0.8 × P(valuation > ask) × (ask − 5.94), peaks around 8. I quote 7.9.

**Bid:** An informed seller only hits the bid when the value is below it, which is rare (about 4%). The bid is therefore also mostly exposed to noise traders. Expected profit is roughly flat between 4.0 and 4.2 and peaks near 4.0–4.2. I quote 4.1.

{"bid": 4.1, "ask": 7.9}

With four heads in four flips, the coin is very likely the always-heads coin. The posterior on that coin is 16/17, which puts the public fair value at about 5.94.

This is the last quote, so I only need to maximise the expected profit on this one trade.

- **Informed trader:** The settlement value is at most 6. The informed trader almost never buys above 6, and sells below about 4.1 only with tiny probability. Quotes far from 6 therefore carry almost no adverse-selection cost.
- **Noise trader:** Valuation is Normal(5.94, 2.6). Expected profit per side is d × P(trade), where d is the distance from fair value. This is maximised at d ≈ 1.9–2.0.

That puts the ask at about 7.9 and the bid at about 4.0.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.9}

info.raw:
Fair value is 6 × (0.5·0.5 + 0.5·1) = 4.5. The settlement value is 6 with probability about 0.51 (the all-heads coin, plus the rare fair-coin 6). Otherwise it is Binomial(6, 0.5), which is centred on 3. Informed traders therefore have a large edge, so I need a wide spread.

I picked the prices by comparing expected profit per quote for several candidates:

- **Ask 5.9:** expected profit is about +0.17. Informed buyers only profit at V = 6, which costs me little at this price, and noise buyers still trade often enough.
- **Bid 2.7:** expected profit is about +0.105. This is roughly the best bid. A higher bid loses too much to informed sellers, and a lower one gives up noise-trader volume.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 5.9}

I priced this from the settlement distribution and the two counterparty types.

**Settlement value:** with probability 1/2 the coin always lands heads, so the value is 6. Otherwise the value is Binomial(6, 0.5). The public fair value is 4.5, and noise traders value the contract at 4.5 + N(0, 1.7).

**Ask:** An informed buyer only buys when the value is 6, so an ask of 6.0 gives up nothing to them. Noise traders still buy about 19% of the time, at an average edge of 1.5 over fair value. That gives an expected profit of about +0.18 per quote, which is better than 5.9 (+0.17) or 6.1 (+0.18) once adverse selection is counted.

**Bid:** The informed side sells to me when the value is low (Binomial outcomes of 2 or fewer). Around 2.7 the noise-trader edge outweighs that loss, for an expected profit of about +0.105 per quote. Nearby bids from 2.5 to 3.0 give almost the same, so I'm keeping 2.7.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

I'm keeping the same quotes as before. The public fair value is 4.5, since the fair coin gives 3 heads in expectation and the always-heads coin gives 6, each with probability 1/2.

- **Ask:** A higher ask avoids losing to informed buyers, who know the value is 6 about half the time. Expected profit per quote is about 0.18 at an ask of 6.0 and a bit lower at 5.9 or 6.1. So 6.0 is close to the best ask.
- **Bid:** Expected profit per quote is about 0.106 at a bid of 2.7 or 2.8. It is lower at 2.0 (about 0.093) and at 3.5 (about 0.04). So 2.7 is close to the best bid.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

The first two flips were both tails. The p=1 coin would never show tails, so the coin must be the fair one. The settlement value is therefore the number of heads in flips 3–6, which is Binomial(4, 0.5) with mean 2.

I checked the expected profit on the ask side, taking an informed trader (probability 0.35) to know the exact value and a noise trader to value the contract at 2 + N(0, 1.7).

| 2.2 | about -0.05 |
| 2.5 | about +0.05 |
| 3.0 | about +0.16 |

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 3.4}

Flips 1 and 2 were both tails, which rules out the coin with P(heads) = 1, so the coin is fair. The settlement value is then the number of heads in flips 3 to 6, which is Binomial(4, 0.5). Its mean, and so the fair value, is 2.0.

To pick the quote I compared expected profit on the ask side at several levels. Informed traders only buy when the value is 3 or 4, which costs me little at a wide ask. Noise traders (sd 1.7) buy rarely but at a good margin.

| 2.5 | about 0.05 |
| 3.0 | about 0.16 |
| 3.4 | about 0.174 |
| 3.5 | about 0.173 |
| 3.7 | about 0.169 |

The best ask is about 3.4. The value distribution is symmetric around 2, so the best bid mirrors it at 0.6. That is the same quote as last time.

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 3.4}

Flips 1 and 2 were both tails, so the coin cannot be the all-heads coin. It must be the fair one. The settlement value is then 0 + 0 + the heads in flips 3–6, which is Binomial(4, 0.5) with a mean of 2.0.

I checked expected profit per quote for an ask at 2 + d, with the bid mirrored at 2 − d:

| d | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | ≈ 0.159 |
| 1.2 | ≈ 0.170 |
| 1.3 | ≈ 0.173 |
| 1.4 | ≈ 0.173 |
| 1.5 | ≈ 0.173 |

Profit is flat for d between 1.3 and 1.5, so I'm keeping the same quote as before, 0.6 / 3.4 (d = 1.4).

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 3.4}

The coin must be the fair one. A coin with P(heads) = 1 would have shown heads on flips 1 and 2, and both were tails. So flips 5 and 6 are each fair, and the settlement value is 2 (from flips 3 and 4) plus the heads in the last two flips. The public fair value is 3.0.

The informed counterparty knows the settlement value exactly. It will be 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25. A noise trader values the contract at 3 + N(0, 1.7).

I compared expected profit at different spreads around 3.0:
- **Tight asks lose money.** At an ask of 3.1 the informed trader buys when the value is 4, costing me 0.9 per trade. That outweighs the small edge from noise traders.
- **Wider asks do better, then flatten.** The expected profit per quote peaks at about 0.19, with the ask between 4.1 and 4.4.
- **The bid mirrors the ask.** Since 3.0 is the fair value, the bid peaks symmetrically, around 1.6 to 1.9.

I'm quoting a symmetric 1.8 / 4.2. My +1 position is well inside the limits, so I'm not skewing the quotes.

{"bid": 1.8, "ask": 4.2}

Flips 1 and 2 were both tails, so the coin can't be the always-heads coin. It must be the fair coin. Flips 3 and 4 gave 2 heads, and flips 5 and 6 are each 50/50, so the expected settlement is 2 + 1 = 3.0.

An informed trader knows the settlement is 2, 3 or 4, with probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4. Quoting too close to 3.0 loses money to informed traders. I checked ask prices from 3.1 upward (the bid is the mirror image around 3.0):

| Ask | Expected edge per quote |

| 3.5 | about +0.08 |
| 3.8 | about +0.15 |
| 4.0 | about +0.18 |
| 4.2 | about +0.19 |
| 4.4 | about +0.19 |

The edge is flat and highest around 4.2 to 4.4. At 4.2 or above, an informed buyer (settlement at most 4) never profits at my ask. I'm marking the position at the expected value of 3.0, so I see no reason to skew the quotes. I'll quote symmetrically around 3.0.

{"bid": 1.8, "ask": 4.2}

Flips 1 and 2 were both tails, so the coin cannot be the P(heads) = 1 coin. It must be the fair coin. The contract then settles at 2 plus the heads from two remaining fair flips, so it is 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25. The expected value is 3.0.

I'm risk-neutral and this is the last quote, so I choose each side to maximise expected profit on that side. Informed traders (probability 0.35) only trade when the value is on the far side of my price. Noise traders (probability 0.65) have valuation 3 + N(0, 1.7).

For the ask at price a, expected profit is 0.35 × P(V > a) × (a − V) plus 0.65 × P(noise > a) × (a − 3). Computed values:

| Ask | Expected profit |

| 3.5 | about 0.08 |

| 4.3 | about 0.188 (maximum) |
| 4.5 | about 0.184 |

At an ask of 4.3 the informed buyer (value at most 4) never trades, so the profit comes only from noise traders. The bid is symmetric around 3.0, so it goes at 1.7.

game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
I set the quote around the prior mean of 4.5 and widened it for adverse selection. The settlement value is 6 with probability about 0.51 (the biased coin, plus the fair coin landing 6 heads). Otherwise it is roughly Binomial(6, 0.5), centred on 3.

- **Ask:** an informed buyer only pays a high price when the value is 6, so I need a high ask. I estimated the expected profit per quote at about 0.18 for an ask of 6.0, against about 0.09 at 5.5. It is about 0.18 at 6.2 too, so 6.0 is near the peak.
- **Bid:** informed sellers appear when the value is low, so I need a low bid. The estimated edge peaks at about 0.10 for a bid between 2.5 and 3.0. I chose 2.7.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

My estimate of the settlement value is about 3.4, down from the 4.5 prior, because the sale at 2.7 is evidence for the fair coin.

- **Why the fill is informative:** A fair-coin informed seller (value ≤ 2) or a noise seller could produce a sale at 2.7. A biased-coin informed trader (value 6) never would. The posterior is about 70% fair coin and 30% all-heads coin, so the expected settlement value is roughly 3.4.
- **Ask:** If the all-heads coin is in play (about 30%), an informed buyer takes any ask below 6. I price the ask where the noise-trader edge outweighs that adverse selection, around 5.3.
- **Bid:** I set the bid near 1.8, where noise-seller edge outweighs informed sellers with low values. I'm already long 1 unit, so I don't want to buy aggressively.

{"bid": 1.8, "ask": 5.3}

My estimate of the fair value is about 3.2, so I'm quoting around that with a spread wide enough to cover informed traders.

- **Prior:** with no information, the expected settlement is 6 × 0.75 = 4.5.
- **Quote 1:** a counterparty sold to me at 2.7. That is more likely to come from a fair coin with few heads, and it moves the fair-coin probability from 0.5 to roughly 0.7.
- **Quote 2:** no trade at 1.8/5.3 is mildly more likely under a fair coin. An informed trader would have bought at 5.3 if the coin were biased. This takes the fair-coin probability to roughly 0.79.
- **Fair value:** given a fair coin I expect about 2.4 heads, because the informed sale suggests a low count. The biased coin gives 6. The blend is about 0.79 × 2.4 + 0.21 × 6 ≈ 3.2.
- **Quotes:** informed buyers hit my ask hard when the value is 6, and informed sellers hit my bid when the value is low. I therefore post a wide spread, centred slightly below the 3.2 fair value because I'm already long one unit.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 4.4}

My estimate of the settlement value is about 5.0, so I'm quoting a wide spread around it.

- **Posterior on the coin:** Two heads are far more likely under the all-heads coin. The history also matters: a seller hit my bid at 2.7, and nobody lifted my 5.3 or 4.4 asks. That points toward the fair coin, so the all-heads coin is only about 51% likely.
- **Fair value:** The two revealed heads are worth 2. The four unrevealed flips are worth 4 × (0.49 × 0.5 + 0.51 × 1) ≈ 3.0. Together that is about 5.0.
- **Ask:** If the value is 6, an informed buyer lifts any ask below 6. An ask near 5.9 costs me little against informed buyers while still earning from noise traders.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers appear when the fair coin lands on a low total. A bid around 3.8 keeps that loss small while still earning from noise sellers. I'm already long one unit, so I'm not bidding higher.

{"bid": 3.8, "ask": 5.9}

My estimate of the settlement value is about 4.7.

- **Flips so far:** Two heads in a row makes the biased coin (P(heads) = 1) much more likely than the fair one.
- **Trade history:** The no-trades at quotes 2–4 point the other way. An informed trader holding a value of 6 would have bought at my asks of 5.3, 4.4 and 5.9, and none did. The sale to me at 2.7 also leans toward the fair coin.
- **Posterior:** Combining these, I put roughly a 1/3 probability on the biased coin.
- **Expected value:** That gives 2 + 0.34 × 4 + 0.66 × 2 ≈ 4.7.

I'm quoting around that value with a spread wide enough to cover informed traders. I'm leaning the ask slightly lower than the bid is below fair value, because I'm already long one unit.

{"bid": 3.9, "ask": 5.4}

Fair value is roughly 3.95, so I'm quoting around that and skewing slightly down because I'm already long 2.

With flips 1 and 2 both heads, the coin is the always-heads one with probability 0.8 on that evidence alone. The settlement value would then be 6, against an expected 4 if the coin is fair, so the flips alone put fair value at about 5.6.

The trading history pulls that down. Informed counterparties only trade at prices that favour them, so I updated on each outcome:
- Quote 5: they sold to me at 3.9, which suggests the value is below 3.9.
- Quote 4: no trade at 3.8/5.9, which suggests the value is inside that range, or that the trader was noise.
- Quotes 1 to 3: a sale at 2.7, then no trades at 1.8/5.3 and 2.5/4.4.

Combining these, the posterior mean settlement value comes to about 3.95. That is well below 5.6 because a fair coin now looks much more likely. The distribution is also wide, with values from 2 to 6 still plausible, so I'm keeping a reasonably wide spread to cover informed traders. Skewing slightly down helps limit more inventory.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 4.4}

Two tails among flips 1–4 mean the coin cannot be the all-heads coin, so it is fair. The settlement value is then 2 plus the heads from flips 5 and 6. That gives 2 with probability 25%, 3 with 50% and 4 with 25%, so the expected value is 3.

For the ask, I compared the expected profit per quote at several prices. The informed trader (35%) only buys when the value is 4, and noise traders (65%) have valuation 3 + N(0, 1.7).
- Ask 3.5: about +0.08
- Ask 4.0: about +0.18
- Ask 4.2: about +0.19
- Ask 4.5: about +0.18

The profit peaks near 4.2–4.3. The bid is the mirror image, so about 1.8. I'm risk-neutral and the +2 position is a modest size, so I'm keeping the quote symmetric around 3.

{"bid": 1.8, "ask": 4.2}

The coin must be the fair one, since flips 3 and 4 were tails and the P(heads)=1 coin can't produce tails. Flips 1 and 2 were heads, so the settlement value is 2 plus the number of heads in flips 5 and 6. That makes the public fair value 3.0. An informed trader knows the value is 2, 3 or 4, with probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4.

Because the distribution is symmetric around 3, I optimised the ask and mirrored the bid. For each ask I computed my expected profit from noise traders (valuation 3 + N(0, 1.7²)) and from informed traders:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 3.6 | about 0.106 |
| 4.0 | about 0.181 |
| 4.3 | about 0.188 |
| 4.5 | about 0.184 |

The optimum is flat around 4.3. Below 4, informed buyers who know the value is 4 take the ask at a loss. At 4.3 and above I avoid informed trades entirely and only fill noise traders. The mirrored bid is 1.7.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Settlement is 6 if the coin is the all-heads coin, otherwise Binomial(6, 0.5), so the expected value is 4.5. The informed trader is the main risk, because the all-heads outcome (probability about 0.51) makes V = 6 very likely.

- **Ask:** at 6.0 an informed buyer can never profit, since V is at most 6. Noise traders still buy about 12% of the time at a margin of roughly 1.5 over fair value. That gives about +0.18 expected profit per quote, better than lower asks, which lose more to informed buyers.
- **Bid:** around 2.7 balances the noise-trader edge against informed sellers, giving about +0.10 expected profit.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

Before any flips are revealed, the settlement value is 3 expected heads if the coin is fair and 6 if it is biased. That gives a fair value of 4.5, with a standard deviation of about 1.7.

I picked each price by comparing the noise-trader gain against the informed-trader loss:

- **Ask:** An informed trader buys whenever the value is 6, which happens with probability about 0.51. Edge falls as the ask drops below 6. At 5.5 the net edge is about 0.09, at 5.9 about 0.17, and at 6.0 about 0.18. An ask of 6.0 avoids the informed loss because a value of 6 does not exceed it. Raising it above 6.0 only reduces the noise fill rate.
- **Bid:** The informed side sells when the coin is fair and the heads count is low. The net edge peaks at about 0.106 for a bid near 2.7 and falls off on either side. At 3.5 it is only about 0.04.

I'm already long 1, but the edge is flat enough near these prices that I'm not shading further.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

The two revealed flips (1 then 0) rule out the all-heads coin, so the coin is fair. Settlement is therefore 1 + Binomial(4, 0.5), with mean 3.0 and values from 1 to 5.

I picked the quotes by comparing expected profit per quote, using noise valuations of N(3, 1.7) and a 35% chance of an informed trader. I also leaned both sides lower because I'm long +2, which makes selling more useful than buying.

- **Ask:** expected profit is near its peak around 4.2–4.5. I chose 4.2, a little below the peak, to favour reducing my long position.
- **Bid:** the symmetric optimum is about 1.6. I moved it down to 1.5 so I'm less likely to add more inventory.

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 4.2}

Flip 1 was heads and flip 2 was tails, so the coin can't be the all-heads one. It must be the fair coin. The expected settlement is 1 + 4 × 0.5 = 3.0.

For the remaining four flips, an informed trader's value is 1 + Binomial(4, 0.5), which ranges from 1 to 5. Noise traders value the contract at about 3.0 with sd 1.7.

Checking expected profit per quote on the ask side, the best asks are 4.2 to 4.5, where noise-trader gains are large and informed losses small. By symmetry the best bids are 1.5 to 1.8. I'm long +2, so I skew both prices slightly lower to favour selling. That gives a bid of 1.7 and an ask of 4.2.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.2}

The revealed flips (1, 0, 0, 0) include tails, so the coin cannot be the always-heads coin. It is the fair coin. The settlement value is 1 + flip 5 + flip 6, so its expected value is 2.0.

An informed trader knows the value is 1, 2 or 3, with probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4. A noise trader's valuation is 2 + N(0, 1.7).

For an ask at 2 + d, I compared the expected profit from noise traders with the expected loss to informed traders:

| Ask | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 2.5 | about 0.08 |
| 3.0 | about 0.18 |
| 3.3 | about 0.19 (the maximum) |
| 3.5 | about 0.18 |

Above 3.0, informed traders never buy because the value is at most 3, so the ask at 3.3 faces only noise traders. The bid is symmetric around 2.0, which gives 0.7.

My long position of +2 leaves room on both sides, so I quote both.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The contract's expected value is 4.5. The coin is fair or all-heads with equal probability, so the mean is 0.5 × 3 + 0.5 × 6.

I picked the quotes by estimating expected profit per quote against the mix of informed (0.35) and noise (0.65, valuation 4.5 + N(0, 1.7)) counterparties.

- **Ask:** An informed buyer only trades when the value is 6, which costs me 6 minus my ask. Noise buyers pay well above 4.5. Expected profit was about 0.17 at an ask of 5.9 and about 0.18 at 6.0, falling again above 6.1, so I use 6.0.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers lose me money whenever the value is below my bid. Noise sellers make it back. Expected profit is flat at about 0.10 for bids between 2.5 and 3.0, so I use 2.7.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

Fair value is 6 × (0.5 × 0.5 + 0.5 × 1) = 4.5, and the settlement value is skewed: it is 6 with probability about 0.51. I compared expected profit across candidate prices on each side. This weighs noise-trader fills, which earn the gap to 4.5, against informed fills, which lose.

- **Ask:** profit is highest around 6.0, at about 0.18 per quote. Informed buyers can't gain above 6, and noise buyers still pay a large edge.
- **Bid:** profit is flat and highest around 2.7, at about 0.105 per quote. Informed sellers hit it only when the value is 2 or less.

I'm keeping the same quotes as before.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

Flip 1 = 0 rules out the coin with P(heads) = 1, because that coin could never show tails. So the coin is fair.

The settlement value is the one revealed head plus the heads in flips 3–6. Those four unrevealed flips average 2 heads, so the expected settlement value is 3.0. The settlement value ranges from 1 to 5 (1 + Binomial(4, 0.5)).

To pick a spread, I compared my expected profit on each side at different distances d from 3.0. A noise trader pays me about d when they trade. An informed trader costs me the amount by which the settlement value is beyond my price. This gives roughly:

| d | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | 0.16 |
| 1.4 | 0.17 |
| 2.0 | 0.16 |

The profit is highest around d ≈ 1.4, so I quote 1.6 / 4.4.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 4.4}

Flip 1 was tails, so the coin cannot be the all-heads coin. It is fair, and the contract is 1 head already revealed plus the expected 2 heads from flips 3–6, giving a base value of 3.

The earlier trade (they bought at 4.4) slightly raises the fair value. Only an informed trader who knew all four remaining flips were heads (value 5) or a high-noise trader would buy there. That puts roughly a 14% chance on value 5, so my fair value is about 3.28.

I solved for the quotes that maximise expected profit against the mix of informed and noise traders. The best ask is high, around 4.5–5, and the best bid is low, around 1.7–2.3. I nudge the bid up a little to 2.1 because I am short and would like to buy back.

{"bid": 2.1, "ask": 4.6}

The coin is fair. A tail has already shown up in the revealed flips, so the always-heads coin is ruled out. The settlement value is therefore 1 head (from flip 2) plus the heads in flips 5 and 6, which averages 1. The public fair value is 2.0.

An informed trader knows the settlement is 1, 2 or 3, with probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4. An informed trader loses me money when they buy below 3 or sell above 1. Noise traders value the contract at 2 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 1.7.

I compared expected profit for symmetric quotes at 2 ± d:
- d = 0.5 gives about 0.081.
- d = 1.0 gives about 0.181.
- d = 1.3 gives about 0.188, the maximum.
- d = 1.5 gives about 0.184.

A spread of about 1.3 on each side balances the edge from noise traders against the loss to informed traders.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.3}

Three of the four revealed flips are tails, and a coin with P(heads) = 1 could never produce a tail, so the coin must be the fair one. One head has already shown, and flips 5 and 6 each contribute 0.5 on average, so the fair value is 2.0.

Flips 5 and 6 give the settlement value 1, 2 or 3 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25. That is the informed trader's knowledge. Noise traders value the contract at 2 + N(0, 1.7).

This is the last quote, so I just maximise expected profit on this one trade. Take the ask as 2 + d:
- Noise traders contribute 0.65 × d × P(Z > d/1.7).
- Informed traders only cost me anything when d < 1, through the value-3 case.
- Net profit is about 0.18 for d between 1.2 and 1.4 and peaks near d = 1.3.

An ask of 3.3 is therefore about optimal. The bid is symmetric, at 0.7.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Before any reveals, the contract's expected settlement is 4.5. That is 0.5 × 3 for the fair coin plus 0.5 × 6 for the all-heads coin.

The main risk is adverse selection from informed traders:
- **Ask side:** If the coin is all heads, the contract settles at 6, so an informed buyer takes any ask below 6 and costs me money. At an ask of 5.9 the informed loss is small, and noise traders still pay a margin over 4.5.
- **Bid side:** If the coin is fair, the value is roughly 3 ± 1.2, so informed sellers hit low bids. Around 3.0 the expected edge from noise sellers outweighs the informed loss.

Checking expected profit per quote, the ask is best near 5.9–6.0 (about +0.11 at 5.9) and the bid near 3.0 (about +0.04).

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 5.9}

Without any revealed flips, the public fair value is 6 × (0.5×0.5 + 0.5×1) = 4.5.

The informed counterparty knows the settlement value V. V is 6 with probability about 0.51, and otherwise it is roughly Binomial(6, 0.5) centred on 3. That makes the ask the riskier side, because an informed buyer wins whenever V = 6.

I compared the expected profit of several quotes, using the 0.35 informed share and the noise trader's valuation of 4.5 + N(0, 1.3).

- **Ask:** Expected profit is negative at 5.0, about +0.05 at 5.5, +0.11 at 5.9, and +0.12 at 6.0. Above 6.0 it declines because noise traders buy less often. At 6.0 an informed buyer has no edge, since V = 6 is not above the ask. The best ask is about 6.0.
- **Bid:** Expected profit is about +0.04 at 3.0, +0.03 at 2.8 and 3.2, and about 0 at 3.5. The best bid is about 3.0.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

I'm keeping the same quotes. The public fair value is 6 × (0.5×0.5 + 0.5×1) = 4.5.

**Ask.** An informed buyer pays off mainly when the coin is all-heads and the value is 6, which has probability 0.5. Comparing noise-trader gains against that informed loss, my expected profit per quote rises as the ask goes up to about 5.9. At 5.9 it is roughly +0.11. At 5.5 it is only about +0.05.

**Bid.** An informed seller hits me when the coin is fair and the heads count lands below my bid. At a bid of 3.0 the expected profit is about +0.04. At 2.5 it is about +0.03, and at 3.5 it is about 0.

Both quotes are slightly positive in expectation, so I'm leaving them as they were.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 5.9}

Public fair value: after two heads, the posterior is 0.8 for the always-heads coin and 0.2 for the fair coin. That gives an expected settlement of 2 + 0.8×4 + 0.2×2 = 5.6.

- **Ask:** An informed buyer almost always knows the value is 6. Any ask below 6 loses money to them, so I quote above 6, near the best expected-profit point of about 6.5 against noise traders.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers only appear when the fair coin runs low, so the bid has less adverse selection. A bid of about 4.4 balances noise-trader profit against those informed losses, and it would also reduce my short position.

{"bid": 4.4, "ask": 6.5}

My estimate of fair value is about 5.85, so I'm quoting a bid below it and an ask above it.

**Coin posterior.** Flips 1 and 2 were both heads. Starting from a 50/50 prior, the posterior on the all-heads coin is 0.8.

**Trade history.** The stage 1 buyer paid my ask of 5.9. A buyer at that price is much more likely if the coin is all-heads, because then an informed trader knows the value is 6. That moves the posterior to about 0.94. My stage 2 quote went untrade, which is slightly more likely if the coin is fair, so it eases the posterior back to about 0.92.

**Fair value.** The 2 revealed heads plus the expected heads in the 4 unrevealed flips gives 2 + 0.92×4 + 0.08×2 ≈ 5.85.

**Ask.** The settlement value is at most 6, so an informed trader never pays more than 6. Any ask above 6 loses only to noise traders, and I sell to them above fair value. Maximising expected profit against noise traders puts the ask around 6.7.

**Bid.** An informed seller only appears if the coin is fair, which is now unlikely, so the adverse-selection cost is small. Noise traders sell to me below fair value. I'm short 1, so buying is also welcome. A bid near 5.2 balances edge against fill probability.

{"bid": 5.2, "ask": 6.7}

My estimate of the settlement value is about 5.9, using flips 1 and 2 as heads, the trade history, and a rough Bayesian update.

**Coin posterior.** Two heads give odds of 4:1 for the biased coin over the fair one. The history pushes that further:
- At quote 3 someone bought at 5.9, which is much more likely if the coin is biased, because then an informed trader knows the value is 6.
- At quotes 4 and 5 nobody sold to my bids of 4.4 and 5.2, which is also more likely if the coin is biased.
- Together these put the biased coin at roughly 96%.

**Fair value.** That gives 2 + 4 × 0.96 + 2 × 0.04 ≈ 5.9, and the value can never exceed 6.

**Ask.** An ask below 6 loses money to an informed buyer when the coin is biased. An ask above 6 is profitable whenever it fills. I'll ask 6.7, which trades the expected profit per fill against the chance of a noise trader's valuation exceeding it.

**Bid.** I'm short one unit, so buying back is welcome. A bid of 5.3 gives a good edge against the roughly 5.9 value and limits losses to an informed seller, who would only appear if the coin is fair.

{"bid": 5.3, "ask": 6.7}

With four heads in four flips, the posterior that the coin is the all-heads coin is 16/17 (about 0.94). The expected number of heads in the last two flips is then 33/17, so the expected settlement value is about 5.94.

- **Informed counterparty:** it knows the value, which is 6 with probability about 0.96, and 5 or 4 otherwise. An ask near 6 gives away too much to informed buyers.
- **Noise trader:** its valuation is roughly 5.94 plus noise with standard deviation 1.3. A wide quote still earns a good edge from noise traders who cross it.
- **Ask:** my rough expected-profit estimates peak at an ask of about 7, and I quote 6.9.
- **Bid:** I am short one unit, so buying back is welcome. My estimates peak around 5.0, where informed sellers are rare because the value is almost always 6, and I quote 5.1.

{"bid": 5.1, "ask": 6.9}

The posterior after four heads in four flips puts the biased coin at 16/17, so the expected settlement value is about 4 + 33/17 ≈ 5.94.

- **Informed traders:** They almost always know the value is 6, or 5 or 4 with small probability. Selling to me below 6 would cost them money, so an ask above 6 is never hit by an informed trader. A bid below 5 is rarely hit by an informed trader either.
- **Noise traders:** Their valuation is about N(5.94, 1.3). A wide ask near 6.8 and a bid near 5.0 give the best expected edge against them, each roughly 0.14 per quote.
- **Position:** I am short 1, so a bid that can buy back is welcome. The risk is small, and both sides have positive edge against the expected value.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 6.8}

Posterior after four heads: P(biased coin) = 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.5/16) = 16/17. The expected final count is 4 + 2·(16/17) + 1·(1/17) ≈ 5.94.

This is the last quote, so I'm only maximising the expected profit of this one trade.

- **Ask:** Informed buyers mostly know the value is 6, so any ask below 6 loses money. Against noise traders, expected profit peaks around 6.9 to 7.0, at about 0.14. I'll use 6.9.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers rarely have value below 5, but they lose me money when they do. Noise traders give the most profit around 4.9, at about 0.14 net. I'll use 4.9.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.9}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The contract's unconditional expected value is 4.5. That is 6 flips times a 0.75 average heads probability, since the coin is fair or all-heads with equal odds.

Settlement is 6 with probability about 0.51 and is otherwise spread around 3. This skew means informed traders hurt a tight quote on the ask side (they buy whenever the value is 6) and on the bid side (they sell whenever the value is low).

I compared expected profit at several prices, counting both noise traders (valuation 4.5 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 1.3) and informed traders (35% of arrivals):
- **Ask:** 6.0 is best at roughly +0.12 per quote. An informed buyer gains nothing at 6, because the value cannot exceed 6. Noise buyers still pay 1.5 above fair value. Asks of 5.5 and 5.8 earn less, about +0.05 and +0.10.
- **Bid:** 3.0 is best at roughly +0.04. Higher bids lose too much to informed sellers, and lower bids attract too few noise sellers.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

My estimate of the contract's value is about 2.8, and I'm quoting around it with a spread wide enough to cover informed traders.

Before quote 1 the expected value was 6 × 0.75 = 4.5. The sale at 3 is informative, because an informed trader only sells when the value is below 3, and that happens only with the fair coin and at most 2 heads.

- Probability of a sale if the coin is fair: informed 0.35 × 0.344 = 0.120, plus noise ≈ 0.0405, for 0.1605 in total.
- Probability of a sale if the coin is biased: noise only, ≈ 0.0405.
- Posterior probability that the coin is fair: 0.1605 / 0.201 ≈ 0.8.
- Expected heads given a fair coin and a sale: ≈ 1.98.
- Expected heads given a biased coin: 6.
- Overall expected value: 0.8 × 1.98 + 0.2 × 6 ≈ 2.8.

The value distribution is skewed, with a 20% chance of exactly 6, so informed buyers are a real risk on the ask and I keep it wider. I'm already long, so I keep the bid modest.

{"bid": 2.3, "ask": 3.5}

Quote 3 is the first one where I can price off the trade history, so I estimated the posterior on the coin first.

- **Prior:** the coin is fair (settlement mean 3) or all-heads (settlement 6), each with probability 1/2. That gives a prior fair value of 4.5.
- **Evidence:** both earlier counterparties sold to me at my bid. All-heads is hard to square with that, because an informed trader would never sell when the value is 6. Only noise traders could have sold in that case.
- **Posterior:** after both sells I put roughly 85–87% on the fair coin. The public fair value is then about 0.87×3 + 0.13×6 ≈ 3.4.
- **Position:** I am long 2, so I want to lean toward selling and skew the quote slightly downward.
- **Bid at 2.7:** this is below fair value. Informed sellers in the fair-coin world cost me about 1 each, while noise sellers give me about 0.6 of edge.
- **Ask at 3.8:** this is above fair value and sells down my long. The loss comes from informed buyers when the coin is all-heads, which is only about 4–5% of arrivals. Noise buyers give me edge of about 0.4 or more.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 3.8}

Flips 1 and 2 are both heads. The posterior that the coin is the all-heads one is 1/(1+0.25) = 0.8. Fair value is therefore 2 + 0.8×4 + 0.2×2 = 5.6.

The informed trader's value is distributed as follows:
- 6 with probability about 0.81
- 5 with probability 0.05
- 4 with probability 0.075
- 3 with probability 0.05
- 2 with probability 0.0125

game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.3 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.

info.raw:
I priced off the expected number of heads and the adverse selection from the informed counterparty.

**Fair value.** The coin's average P(heads) is 0.3·0.2 + 0.4·0.3 + 0.5·0.5 = 0.43. Over 6 flips that gives an expected settlement of about 2.58.

**Settlement distribution.** The mixture over the three coins gives roughly:

| Heads | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.045 |
| 1 | 0.163 |
| 2 | 0.275 |
| 3 | 0.276 |
| 4 | 0.171 |
| 5 | 0.060 |
| 6 | 0.009 |

**Choosing the spread.** For each candidate price I added up two effects:
- **Informed trader:** half of arrivals trade against me whenever the true value is beyond my quote, and I lose the difference.
- **Noise trader:** the other half trade when 2.58 plus Normal(0, 1.3) noise crosses my quote, and I gain the distance from 2.58.

On the ask side, the expected profit per quote is about +0.01 at 3.5, +0.059 at 4.0 and +0.054 at 4.2. On the bid side, it is about +0.066 at 1.0, versus +0.056 at 1.2 and +0.058 at 0.8. I take the peaks, a bid of 1.0 and an ask of 4.0. This is a wide spread, but that is what the informed-trader losses require.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 4.0}

My estimate of the settlement value is about 2.67 heads.

- **Prior:** the average heads probability is 0.2×0.3 + 0.3×0.4 + 0.5×0.5 = 0.43, so the expected count over 6 flips is 2.58.
- **Update from quote 1:** a buyer at 4 is more likely to hold a high value, which favours the heavier-heads coins. That raises the average heads probability to about 0.445 and the expected count to about 2.67.
- **Spread:** the value has a standard deviation of roughly 1.2, and half of counterparties are informed, so I keep the spread fairly wide.
- **Position:** I'm short 1, so I lean the quotes slightly toward buying. The bid is closer to fair value than the ask.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 3.2}

My estimate of the settlement value is about 2.08. This is flip 1 (tails, so 0 heads) plus the expected heads in the 5 remaining flips under the coin posterior. That posterior comes from the prior, the tails flip, and the earlier trades, and works out to roughly 27% p=0.3, 32% p=0.4 and 42% p=0.5.

Informed buyers and sellers have real edge here because the heads count is spread over 0 to 5. I compared expected profit per quote at several bid and ask levels. Against informed traders, the best bid is just below the 0-heads outcome (about 0.9), and the best ask sits near 3.3 to 3.5.

I'm quoting wide on both sides. My position is flat, so there is no need to skew.

{"bid": 0.9, "ask": 3.4}

My estimate of the fair value is about 1.2, well below the unconditioned 2.1, because the trade history is informative.

- **Flip 1 = 0:** Updating the coin prior on this gives an expected final count of about 2.1.
- **Trade history:** The last three trades shift this down. The sale at my 0.9 bid is most likely an informed trader who knew the count was 0, since a noise trader would rarely sell that low. Weighting each trade by how likely it is under informed and noise valuations pulls the fair value to about 1.2.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers at the bid lose me money. The best bid is therefore very low, around 0.1, where I only really catch noise sellers.
- **Ask:** Informed buyers are costly at low asks. An ask near 2.8 is high enough to avoid most informed buys and still gets some noise flow. It also helps reduce my long position.

{"bid": 0.1, "ask": 2.8}

After five tails, flips 1 to 5 contribute nothing, so the contract is worth only flip 6.

**Posterior on the coin.** The likelihood of five tails is 0.7⁵ = 0.168 for the 0.3 coin, 0.6⁵ = 0.0778 for the 0.4 coin and 0.5⁵ = 0.03125 for the 0.5 coin. Weighting by the priors 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5 gives 0.0336, 0.0233 and 0.0156, which sum to 0.0726. The expected P(heads) is therefore about 0.375, which is the public fair value.

**Ask.** The informed trader buys only if the value is 1, and an ask below 1 loses money to it. At an ask of about 1.4 the informed trader never buys, and only noise traders do. The expected profit per quote is then 0.5 × P(noise valuation > 1.4) × (1.4 − 0.375) ≈ 0.11, close to the peak. An ask of 0.9 earns only about 0.07.

**Bid.** The informed trader sells only when the value is 0, so any bid above 0 loses to it. A bid of 0.1 earns about 0.03 and a bid of 0 about 0.07. A bid of −0.6 avoids the informed trader entirely and earns about 0.5 × 0.227 × 0.975 ≈ 0.11 from noise traders.

Being long 2 is well inside the ±4 limit and the objective is expected profit, so I post the wide quotes.

{"bid": -0.6, "ask": 1.4}

Flips 1–5 were all tails, so the settlement value is just flip 6, which is 0 or 1.

**Posterior on the coin** (prior × likelihood of 5 tails):
- P(heads) = 0.3: 0.2 × 0.7⁵ = 0.0336
- P(heads) = 0.4: 0.3 × 0.6⁵ = 0.0233
- P(heads) = 0.5: 0.5 × 0.5⁵ = 0.0156

Normalised, these are 0.463, 0.322 and 0.215. The expected P(heads) is about 0.375, so the fair value is about 0.375.

**Ask.** An informed buyer who knows flip 6 is heads (value 1) buys at any ask below 1 and costs me money. An ask of 1 or more avoids that. Only noise traders, with valuation 0.375 + N(0, 1.3), then buy. Maximising (a − 0.375) × P(noise valuation > a) gives an ask near 1.3–1.4. The expected profit is about 0.11 either way, so I use 1.3.

**Bid.** An informed seller who knows the value is 0 sells to any bid above 0 and costs me money. A bid at or below 0 avoids that. Maximising (0.375 − b) × P(noise valuation < b) gives a bid near −0.6, again worth about 0.11.

{"bid": -0.6, "ask": 1.3}

info.raw:
Four heads in four flips shifts the coin posterior to about 85% for P(heads) = 0.7. The expected value of the three unseen flips (5, 6 and 7) is then about 20.1, so fair value is roughly 60.1.

The settlement value is 40 plus 10 times the heads in flips 5–7. The informed trader therefore knows it is 40, 50, 60 or 70. I put the probabilities at about 4%, 22%, 43% and 31%.

I compared candidate quotes by their expected profit against both trader types:

- **Ask:** around 70 is best. An informed buyer only profits when the value is 70, and at 70 they gain nothing. Noise buyers still pay about 10 above fair value. That gives roughly +1.2 per quote.
- **Bid:** around 50 is best, by the same reasoning. Informed sellers rarely have value below 50. Noise sellers give about 10 of edge. That gives roughly +1.0 per quote.

My position is flat, so I don't need to skew the quotes.

{"bid": 50.1, "ask": 70.0}

My estimate of the settlement value is about 60.1, and I'm quoting wide around it.

**Posterior on the coin.** All four revealed flips are heads.
- Likelihood for the 0.5 coin is 0.5⁴ = 0.0625, and for the 0.7 coin it is 0.7⁴ = 0.2401.
- Weighting by the priors gives 0.4 × 0.0625 = 0.025 and 0.6 × 0.2401 = 0.144.
- So P(0.7 coin) ≈ 0.852, and the expected heads probability is ≈ 0.670.

**Fair value.** The three unseen flips add about 3 × 0.670 ≈ 2.01 heads. That gives 4 + 2.01 ≈ 6.01 heads, so fair value is about 60.1.

**Settlement distribution.** The settlement value is 40 + 10 × (heads in flips 5–7). Mixing over the two coins:

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 40 | 0.04 |
| 50 | 0.43 |
| 60 | 0.22 |
